pair2223-s3.name: The Anti-Breakthrough with the practice sentence, the last try: from the near miss, "I'd do"
pair2223-s3.text:
The Anti-Breakthrough (Micro-Dosing): A brain stuck in alarm can often take in healing work for only a few seconds at a time, Perry finds. So for now we have to give up on the hour-long breakthrough that therapy aims for, since an hour spent working on the trauma itself overwhelms an armored nervous system more than it heals it. Instead, this protocol works in doses of a few seconds, which is what I mean by micro-dosing here.

In practice, I'd do 30 seconds of slow breathing, twenty times a day.

sw19-s4.name: The one-sixteenth paragraph, step 4 from #312: the closing figure said plainly
sw19-s4.text: That works out to about one-sixteenth of the grown-ups per child that our brains evolved with (Perry, 2023). So the emptiness you feel (the "Void") is real, since it's what that missing company feels like. Once you've de-armored, going back to a lonely life will feel worse than it did with the armor on. Gather a tribe of people you're close to and see most days, or you'll eventually reach for the armor again just to get through the loneliness.
